bullets: Targets factuality and reliability assessment for individual LLM claims under white-box access.
Builds a positive semi-definite token kernel from the model’s conditional distribution and token contradiction scores.
Estimates contradiction using frequency statistics from Wikipedia.
Evaluated on two benchmarks, four European languages, and 16 models; it matches average performance and performs better in high-precision settings.
Runs on CPU while achieving substantial speedups over GPU cross-encoder and comparable CPU-based methods, supporting real-time monitoring.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Example from the MUCH dataset [7]: only one of the nine claims in the LLM generation is incorrect. KTC correctly identifies the wrong price ($1,699), yielding a high uncertainty score for the incorrect claim, while CCP [9] produces several false positives and thus lower precision. Our method computes token-level scores that are aggregated at the claim level (see dashed lines on the plot).

Figure 4: Accuracy–efficiency trade-off for white-box claim-level UQ methods. Each point corresponds to a method evaluated under a different set of hyperparameters. The x-axis reports the UQ computation time as a fraction of the LLM generation cost. KTC achieves competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of NLI-based methods (CCP, SAR), while requiring no GPU.

Figure 3: Illustration of KTC computation for three tokens from the example in Figure 1. (top) candidate tokens and their likelihoods, (centre) the non-contradiction graph, (bottom) the entropy at different stages of the computation. (left) epistemic uncertainty, where the model hesitates between contradicting prices, resulting in a sparse non-contradiction graph and a high KTC score. (centre) aleatoric uncertainty, where the model hesitates between non-contradicting formulations, yielding high conditional entropy but low semantic entropy and thus a low KTC score. (right) low uncertainty, with low conditional entropy; despite high semantic entropy, scaling leads to a low KTC score.

Figure 9: Hyperparameter generalization. Each point corresponds to a method evaluated under a different set of hyperparameters. The x-axis reports the UQ computation time as a fraction of the LLM generation cost. KTC configurations are selected on the manually annotated data and evaluated without retuning on the 4,673 automatically annotated samples in MUCH, showing that the accuracy-efficiency trade-off generalizes to unseen data.

Figure 5: Precision-Recall curves for claim-level hallucination detection across four languages, using product as token-to-claim aggregation method. Results are averaged over 16 LLMs across two benchmarks. KTC notably outperforms competing methods in the high-precision regime (low recall), while remaining competitive overall.

Figure 6: Precision–recall curves for KTC under four token-to-claim aggregation strategies (Mean, Maximum, Geometric mean, Product), averaged across four languages and 16 LLMs. Each method is evaluated over its full grid search space, and we report its best-performing configuration.

Figure 7: ROC curves for claim-level hallucination detection across four languages, using product for token-to-claim aggregation. Results are averaged over 16 LLMs across two benchmarks. Each method is evaluated over its full grid search space, and we report its best-performing configuration.

Figure 8: ROC curves for KTC under four token-to-claim aggregation strategies (Mean, Maximum, Geometric mean, Product), averaged over all four languages and 16 LLMs. Each method is evaluated over its full grid search space, and we report its best-performing configuration.

Figure 2: The KTC score is computed for each LLM-generated token. We construct a noncontradiction graph over candidate tokens (step [A]) and represent it as a PSD semantic kernel (step [B]). This kernel is then combined with the predictive kernel containing candidate probabilities (step [C]). Finally, we compute the Von Neumann entropy (VNE) of the combined kernel (step [D]).
Table 3: Hyperparameter configurations evaluated for each method.

Table 1: Precision–recall AUC of aggregation methods for varying neighbourhood size ν. SCALE consistently outperforms COMB across all configurations. Within COMB, performance peaks around α ∈ [0.5, 0.75], while both extremes (α = 0 and α = 1) yield lower scores. This trend is stable across all ν, which supports the importance of coupling both semantic and predictive kernels.

Table 4: Performance of the evaluated hyperparameter configurations on the base evaluation set (698 manually-annotated samples from MUCH [7] and Mu-SHROOM [33]). Time is relative to LLM generation time.
Table 5: Performance on the test set consisting of the 4,673 automatically annotated samples from MUCH [7]. The KTC configurations are evaluated without retuning.

Table 2: Non-contradiction scores produced by the Wikipedia heuristic. Synonyms and hypernyms receive substantially higher scores than semantically close but non-hypernym concepts, indicating that the heuristic does not simply measure generic semantic similarity. Values are mean ± standard deviation over 100 pairs per category.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight kernel-based claim uncertainty quantification for LLMs with large speedups; relevant to efficient LLM inference and LLM reliability.
papers.title: Kernel Token Contradiction: a Fast and Principled Approach for LLM Claim Uncertainty Quantification
papers.tldr: KTC provides fast, claim-level uncertainty estimates for LLM outputs by combining token probabilities and contradiction signals in a kernel whose uncertainty is measured with Von Neumann entropy.
